find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array.pattern: Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)

approaches.name: Try every divisor from the smallest value down
approaches.idea: Find the minimum and maximum, then test candidates from `min` downwards; the first that divides both is the GCD.
steps: For `d` from `lo` down to 1: if `lo % d == 0` and `hi % d == 0`, return `d`.
approaches.why: One pass for min/max, then up to `min` trial divisions.

approaches.name: Euclid on min and max
approaches.idea: Any common divisor of `a` and `b` also divides `a mod b`, so `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`, ending when the remainder is 0.
approaches.why: The remainders shrink at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers, so Euclid takes O(log) steps.

palindrome-number.pattern: Digit arithmetic: peel digits with % 10 and / 10, reversing only half

approaches.name: Compare the decimal string with its reverse
approaches.idea: Turn the number into a string and check that it equals its reverse. The minus sign makes every negative number fail automatically.
approaches.why: d = number of digits (≤ 10); the string costs O(d) memory, which the follow-up wants to avoid.

approaches.name: Reverse the whole number
approaches.idea: Build the reversed number digit by digit and compare it with the original. Use a 64-bit value, because reversing a large 32-bit number can exceed the 32-bit range.
steps: Pop digits from a copy (`d = n % 10`, `n /= 10`) and push them onto `rev = rev·10 + d`.
approaches.why: One pass over the digits, but it needs a wider integer type to be safe.

approaches.name: Reverse only the second half
approaches.idea: Pop digits from the end into `rev` until `rev` is at least the remaining front part. Then the halves can be compared directly; no overflow is possible because `rev` holds at most half the digits.
steps: Negative numbers, and positive numbers ending in 0, are not palindromes (0 itself is).
Return `x == rev` (even length) or `x == rev / 10` (odd length: drop the middle digit).
approaches.why: Only half the digits are processed, and everything stays inside 32 bits.

approaches.name: Test every number against every smaller divisor
approaches.idea: For each number from 2 to n − 1, check whether any number between 2 and itself divides it.
steps: For each `i` in `[2, n)`: try every `j` in `[2, i)`; `i` is prime if none divides it.
approaches.why: Each prime costs a full scan below it. Hopeless at n = 5·10⁶.

approaches.name: Trial division up to √i
approaches.idea: If `i` has a divisor, it has one no larger than `√i`. So each number only needs divisors up to its square root.
steps: For each `i` in `[2, n)`: try `j` while `j·j ≤ i`.
Count `i` if no such `j` divides it.
approaches.why: Each prime costs √i divisions — still around 10⁹ operations for n = 5·10⁶.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
approaches.idea: Instead of testing numbers, cross out multiples. For each prime `p` (found in increasing order), mark `p², p² + p, …` as composite; smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes.
steps: For `p` from 2 while `p·p < n`: if `p` is not composite, mark every multiple from `p·p` with step `p`.
Count the unmarked numbers in `[2, n)`.
approaches.why: The marking work is n·(1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + …) over primes, which sums to n log log n.

approaches.name: Multiply |n| times
approaches.idea: Multiply `x` by itself |n| times, and take the reciprocal when `n` is negative.
steps: Let `m = |n|` as a 64-bit value (|−2³¹| does not fit in an int).
approaches.why: Up to 2.1·10⁹ multiplications for the extreme exponents.

approaches.name: Recursive halving
approaches.idea: `xⁿ = (x^(n/2))²`, times one extra `x` when `n` is odd. Each call halves the exponent.
steps: `half = power(x, m / 2)`; return `half·half`, times `x` if `m` is odd.
Call it with `m = |n|` (64-bit) and take the reciprocal for negative `n`.
approaches.why: About 31 levels of recursion for any 32-bit exponent.

approaches.name: Iterative binary exponentiation
approaches.idea: Read the exponent in binary: keep squaring a running base, and multiply it into the result whenever the current bit of the exponent is 1.
steps: While `m > 0`: if `m` is odd, `result *= base`; then `base *= base`, `m /= 2`.
approaches.why: One squaring per bit of the exponent and no recursion.

reverse-integer.pattern: Digit popping with an overflow check before each push

approaches.name: Reverse the digit string, check the range
approaches.idea: Reverse the decimal string of |x|, parse it as a 64-bit number, restore the sign, and return 0 if it falls outside the 32-bit range.
steps: Take the digits of |x| as a string (in 64-bit, since |−2³¹| overflows an int) and reverse it.
Parse, apply the sign, and return 0 if the result is outside `[−2³¹, 2³¹ − 1]`.
approaches.why: d ≤ 10 digits. It breaks the "no 64-bit integers" rule, which is what the next approach fixes.

approaches.name: Pop and push digits, checking before overflow
approaches.idea: Pop the last digit with `% 10` and push it onto `rev` with `rev·10 + d`. Before pushing, check that `rev·10 + d` would still fit — using only 32-bit comparisons against `MAX / 10` and `MIN / 10`.
steps: While `x != 0`: `d = x % 10` (it keeps the sign of `x`); `x /= 10`.
If `rev > MAX/10`, or `rev == MAX/10` and `d > 7`, return 0. Likewise if `rev < MIN/10`, or `rev == MIN/10` and `d < −8`.
`rev = rev·10 + d`. Return `rev` at the end.
approaches.why: One step per digit and never a value outside 32 bits. Python and JavaScript have no 32-bit overflow, so the same checks are done against the explicit limits.

factorial-trailing-zeroes.pattern: Legendre's formula: count factors of 5 via n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + …

approaches.name: Compute n! exactly and count zeros
approaches.idea: Build n! as a big integer and count how many times it ends in 0.
steps: Multiply 1 × 2 × … × n with arbitrary-precision arithmetic (C++: an array of base-10⁹ limbs).
approaches.why: n! has about n·log₁₀ n digits and every multiplication touches all of them.

approaches.name: Count factors of 5 in each number
approaches.idea: Each trailing zero is a factor 10 = 2 × 5, and factors of 2 are always more plentiful. So count how many 5s divide each of 1..n.
steps: For each `i` from 5 to n (step 5): while `i` is divisible by 5, divide and count.
approaches.why: n/5 numbers, each divided by 5 at most log₅ n times — about n/4 divisions in total.

approaches.name: Count multiples of 5, 25, 125, …
approaches.idea: `n / 5` numbers contribute at least one 5, `n / 25` contribute a second, `n / 125` a third, and so on. Summing those counts gives every factor of 5 exactly once.
approaches.why: The loop runs log₅ n times. Dividing `n` itself (instead of growing a power of 5) avoids overflow.

approaches.name: Multiply position by position
approaches.idea: Each even index has 5 choices and each odd index has 4, independently. Multiply them one position at a time, modulo 10⁹ + 7.
steps: For `i` from 0 to n − 1: multiply by 5 if `i` is even, otherwise by 4 (mod 10⁹ + 7).
approaches.why: n can be 10¹⁵, so a loop over positions is far too slow.

approaches.name: 5^⌈n/2⌉ · 4^⌊n/2⌋ with fast power
approaches.idea: There are ⌈n/2⌉ even indices and ⌊n/2⌋ odd ones, so the answer is `5^⌈n/2⌉ · 4^⌊n/2⌋ mod 10⁹ + 7`. Compute each power by repeated squaring.
steps: `power(b, e)`: square-and-multiply on the bits of `e`, reducing mod 10⁹ + 7 each step.
approaches.why: About 50 squarings for n = 10¹⁵. Products of two values below 10⁹ + 7 need 64 bits; JavaScript uses BigInt because they exceed 2⁵³.

approaches.name: Draw from a shrinking pool
approaches.idea: Copy the values into a pool. Repeatedly pick a random element of the pool, append it to the result and remove it. Every order is equally likely, but removing from the middle of a list costs O(n).
steps: `shuffle`: copy the array into a list; n times, remove a uniformly random index and append that value.
`reset`: return a copy of the original.
approaches.why: Each shuffle does n removals, each shifting up to n elements.

approaches.name: Fisher–Yates (Knuth) shuffle
approaches.idea: Shuffle a copy in place: for `i` from the end down to 1, swap position `i` with a uniformly random position `j` in `[0, i]`. Each value ends up in each slot with equal probability.
steps: `shuffle`: copy it; for `i` from n − 1 down to 1, pick `j` uniformly in `[0, i]` and swap `a[i]` with `a[j]`.
`reset`: return a copy of the original.
approaches.why: n − 1 swaps per shuffle. There are n·(n − 1)·…·1 = n! equally likely choice sequences, one per permutation — so it is exactly uniform. (Picking `j` from the whole array instead is a classic bug that biases the result.)

linked-list-random-node.pattern: Reservoir sampling (pick from a stream of unknown length)

approaches.name: Copy the values into an array
approaches.idea: Store every value in an array once; each call picks a random index.
steps: Constructor: walk the list and append each value to an array.
`getRandom`: return the value at a uniformly random index.
approaches.why: O(n) to build, then O(1) per call — but it keeps a full copy of the list, which the follow-up rules out.

approaches.name: Count once, then walk to a random index
approaches.idea: Keep only the head and the length. Each call picks a random index and walks to it.
steps: Constructor: store `head` and count the nodes.
`getRandom`: pick `k` uniformly in `[0, length)` and step `k` times from the head.
approaches.why: O(n) per call and O(1) extra space — but it needs the length up front, which a true stream does not give you.

approaches.name: Reservoir sampling
approaches.idea: Walk the list once; when you reach the i-th node (1-based), make it the current pick with probability 1/i. Node i survives the later nodes with probability `i/(i+1) · (i+1)/(i+2) · … · (n−1)/n`, so every node ends up chosen with probability exactly 1/n.
steps: `getRandom`: for `i = 1, 2, …` over the nodes, replace `result` with the node's value when `random(0..i−1) == 0`.
approaches.why: One pass per call, O(1) memory, and no need to know the length in advance — the setting the follow-up asks about.

implement-rand10-using-rand7.pattern: Rejection sampling (and recycling the rejected randomness)

approaches.name: A uniform 1..5 and a fair coin
approaches.idea: Reject 6 and 7 to get a uniform 1..5, and reject 7 to get a fair coin from 1..6 (odd/even). Together they give 10 equally likely outcomes.
approaches.why: Expected calls to rand7: 7/5 + 7/6 ≈ 2.57. The number of calls is unbounded in the worst case, but each retry is independent, so it ends with probability 1.

approaches.name: 7 × 7 grid, keep the first 40
approaches.idea: Two calls give a uniform number 1..49 via `(rand7() − 1)·7 + rand7()`. Keep 1..40 (four copies of 1..10) and retry on 41..49.
approaches.why: Each try uses 2 calls and succeeds with probability 40/49, so the expected cost is 2·49/40 ≈ 2.45 calls.

approaches.name: Rejection sampling that recycles the leftover
approaches.idea: A rejected value is still uniform over what was left: 41..49 is a uniform 1..9. Combine it with another rand7 to get 1..63 (keep 60), then the rejected 61..63 is a uniform 1..3; combine again for 1..21 (keep 20). Only 21 restarts from scratch.
approaches.why: Wasting less randomness lowers the expected cost to about 2.19 calls per result — the lowest of these three schemes.
